newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia rejects compensation to Stolen Generation.
newsitem.headline: Australia rejects compensation to Stolen Generation.

text.p: Australia has rejected calls to pay compensation to tens of thousands of Aborigines forcibly removed as children from their parents under an assimilation policy labelled by a human rights report as attempted genocide.

But Aborigines and Australia's Human Rights Commission on Thursday warned that reconciliation between white and black Australia, now strained because of a bitter race debate, rested on the acknowledgment and compensation of past injustices.
Attorney General Daryl Williams said that the government opposed compensation, quoting the government's submission to the human rights inquiry into the "Stolen Generation" Aborigines.

"The government can see no equitable or practical way of now paying special compensation to those persons, if compensation were considered to be warranted," said Williams on Wednesday, quoting from the submission which has not been made public.

A 700-page report by Australia's Human Rights Commission titled "Bringing them Home" labels the assimilation policy "genocidal" and calls on the government to apologise and pay compensation, according to leaked extracts of the report.
The leaked extracts said Australia was obliged to pay compensation under international human rights laws.

"Systematic racial discrimination and genocide must not be trivialised and Australia's obligation under international law to make reparations must not be ignored," said the report, according to The Australian newspaper.
Williams rejected the genocide finding, saying it was "flawed and wrong" because the assimilation policy was not intended to destroy a racial group.
He said that while the government acknowledged that the policy of assimilation which existed from the 1880s to the 1960s was misguided, it would not condem it.
"To now attribute malice to their actions would be a distortion of history," Williams said in a statement.
"However much we may now think those actions to have been misguided and misplaced, it is unfair and unjust to now malign their intentions," he said.

President of Australia's Human Rights Commission, Sir Ron Wilson, has called the assimilation policy a deliberate attempt to breed out Aborigines. "It clearly was attempted genocide. It was believed that the Aboriginal people would die out," he said.

The Commission said in a statement on Thursday that its report does not attribute malice to the governments involved in the assimilation policy, but calls on the present government to accept responsibility for its legacy.

"Acknowledgment, apology, recognition and reassurance that these policies will never again be endorsed by governments and welfare systems are the fundamental keys to reconciliation," the Commission said.

The author of the human rights report, Social Justice Commissioner Mick Dodson, says Aboriginal Australia is today dysfunctional as a result of the separation policy, with family breakdowns endemic and drug and alcohol abuse widespread.

"No longer will we allow the experiences of the removal of Aboriginal people to be ignored, dismissed and swept under the carpet," said the Link-Up Aboriginal Corporation, which works to reunite Aborigines separated from their parents.
"We can never be reconciled as a nation until our life experiences have been acknowledged,"
It remained unclear whether the government would apologise as Prime Minister John Howard last year told parliament Australians should not feel guilty about the past.
Williams said the report will be tabled in parliament next week and the government's aboriginal affairs minister will issue a full response to the report.
